fields.meta_title: Drug Test Consent Form for Employers | Emergent
fields.meta_description: What a drug test consent form covers, where DOT rules differ, and an app that collects signatures on a phone and limits who sees each result.
fields.h1: Build a Drug Test Consent Form
fields.hero_description: A drug test consent form records that someone agreed to a test and who may receive the result. Emergent builds the form and the record HR works from.
fields.explore_cta: Build My Drug Test Consent Form
fields.features_heading: Every Signature Tied to a Test
fields.features_subheading: A printed slip proves someone signed once. Emergent's version knows which test the signature covered and who may read the result.
fields.feature_1:
Consent on a single screen

Shows the consent text your counsel approved on one screen, with the test type and reason filled in. The signer types a name and signs, and the time lands on the record.
fields.feature_2:
A reason recorded for each test

Logs why each test happened: pre-employment, random selection, post-accident or reasonable suspicion. Every reason carries its own wording in the text the signer sees.
fields.feature_3:
Releases that name the recipient

Asks who may receive the result and stores that list with the signature. Anyone left off it, the supervisor included, sees that the test happened and never the result.
fields.feature_4:
Clinic hand-off by API

Sends the signed consent and a collection authorization to the clinic or lab you use. Results return to that same record through its API without anyone retyping a name.
fields.feature_5:
Reminders until the last signature

Emails anyone in a random pool or a school program who has not signed yet. Reminders follow the schedule you set and stop the moment a signature arrives on the record.
fields.feature_6:
Code that belongs to you

Exports the full codebase to your GitHub on paid plans. Your engineers can host the app on your own servers or connect it to the HRIS your company runs for payroll and benefits.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Programs That Need a Signature First
fields.tab_content_1:
A signed consent and a clinic slot the same afternoon

Conditional offers at Harbor Point Distribution end with a link, not a clipboard. The new order picker signs the consent on her phone in the lobby and picks a collection site near home. Dana Ruiz in HR sees the signed form at 2:31 PM, and the clinic receives an authorization that stays open for 48 hours.
fields.tab_content_2:
No unsigned names left in the random pool

Random pools only work when every name in them has acknowledged the policy. Cascade Plastics put 214 plant employees in its pool, and 197 have signed. The other 17 get an email reminder every 2 days, and a name joins the draw only after its signature lands.
fields.tab_content_3:
Results seen by one named HR manager

Forklift contact with a rack at Globex Packaging starts the post-accident process. The shift supervisor opens the form on a tablet at the scene, and the operator signs it there. The release names Omar Haddad in HR as the only person who receives the result, and the supervisor's view stops at Collected.
fields.tab_content_4:
Every athlete cleared or flagged before Friday's game

Pine Valley School District tests athletes at random, and a parent signs for each one. Of 140 athletes on fall rosters, 112 have a signed parent form. The athletic director gets the eligibility list on Thursday at 4 PM, with the 28 unsigned names flagged for coaches to chase.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Drug Test Consent Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps for an employer or school writing its own form, starting with whether a federal rule already governs the test.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Name the test and the reason
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide which tests the form covers. DOT-required urine tests are documented on the federal custody and control form, and 49 CFR 40.27 bars the employer from requiring a separate consent or release for any DOT test. Your own form fits non-DOT programs.
fields.howto_step_2_des: State rules differ. Minnesota, for one, allows testing only under a written policy that meets its minimum contents. Have counsel confirm what your state requires before the form goes live, and change the form whenever the policy changes.
fields.howto_step_3_des: State the sample type, such as urine or breath, and why the test is happening: pre-employment, random, post-accident or reasonable suspicion. A signer should understand what they agreed to without opening the policy manual.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Name the people or roles who may see the result, such as one HR manager and the collection clinic. Keep that list short. Everyone outside it should see only whether the sample was collected, not what the lab found.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Capture a typed or drawn signature with a timestamp on each form. For minors in a school program, a parent or guardian signs. Store the signed copy on the person's record, apart from the general personnel file.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Give every person a status: link sent, signed, collected, result in. Remind anyone who has not signed after a couple of days, and keep unsigned employees out of a random selection until their acknowledgment is on file.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Store results where only the named recipients can open them. Agree on a retention period with counsel and delete results when it ends. Keep each consent for as long as you keep the result it covers.

plan.angle: The top results are printable PDFs from single employers, schools and collection sites: a paragraph of consent and a signature line. None says which tests need the employer's own form and which do not. This page draws that line first: DOT-covered tests run on the federal custody form and the employer may not demand a separate consent, while non-DOT programs rely on the employer's form and, in some states, a written policy. Then it builds what a PDF cannot: signatures on a phone, a release that names who sees the result, an acknowledgment count for a random pool, and a parent signature trail for school programs.

claims_to_source: In DOT-regulated testing, an employer must not require an employee to sign a consent, release, waiver of liability or indemnification agreement for any part of the testing process

Under 49 CFR 40.25, an employer must get the employee's written consent and request drug and alcohol testing records from DOT-regulated employers from the previous two years before the employee first performs safety-sensitive duties, and an employee who refuses consent cannot perform those duties

Under 49 CFR 40.321, individual DOT test results may not be released to third parties without the employee's specific written consent naming the information, the recipient and the time; blanket releases are prohibited
DOT drug tests must use the Federal Drug Testing Custody and Control Form; employers may not use a non-federal form for a DOT test
Under EEOC guidance on the ADA, a test to determine the current illegal use of drugs is generally not a medical examination
Minnesota employers may not request or require a drug or alcohol test unless it follows a written testing policy that meets the state's minimum contents
